cases.text: The goal of Save for later is to help readers come back and actually finish articles they don't have time for right now. Key actions: saving an article, and returning to open a saved article. Metrics: articles saved per weekly reader, and the share of saved articles opened within 7 days. The most important is the share opened within 7 days, because saves alone don't show anyone came back to read.

I'd start with what the button is for: letting people park a story and read it later instead of losing it. Users can tap save, and later open their saved list and read a story to the end. I'd count saves per active user per week, and how many saved stories get read to the end. The one I'd watch is saved stories read to the end, since that's the button doing its job.
I'd track DAU, time spent and total saves, plus engagement on the saved list. If those numbers go up after launch, the button works.
Success means more people love the app. I'd run a survey asking if users like the new button and check our app store ratings.
The button should help readers finish articles they didn't have time for. People save articles and come back to them later. I'd look at saves per user and overall engagement with the saved list.
I'd track articles saved per weekly user and how many saved articles get opened within a week. The second matters most. The goal is to get people reading more.

North Star: weekly agents who send at least one AI-drafted reply, a count of people getting value. Guardrail: customer escalation rate must not rise, because pushing drafts onto more tickets could let wrong answers reach customers. And I'd track override rate: how often agents heavily edit or discard a draft, which shows whether they trust it.

Rather than average CSAT, which can rise just because the AI only gets easy tickets, I'd count tickets resolved using an AI draft each week. I'd hold reopen rate flat as we expand, so faster replies don't come at the cost of wrong ones. If agents rewrite most drafts from scratch, that tells us they don't trust them.
Our North Star is average CSAT on AI-drafted tickets, and we'd push drafts onto as many tickets as possible to maximize it.
I'd measure the accuracy of the drafts on a test set and track overall engagement with the feature.
North Star: the number of agents sending AI drafts each week. We'd also keep an eye on hallucination rate.
The North Star stays average CSAT on AI tickets. As we expand drafts, escalations must not go up, since bad drafts would reach customers. I'd also watch how often agents discard drafts.

Scope: small sellers on our marketplace using the AI description writer, over the first 8 weeks after launch. Secondary: share of AI descriptions published without edits, and listings published per seller per week. Business: sales on listings with AI descriptions, and cost per description generated. Tracking: 'published without edits' is a description saved unchanged before publishing, logged as an app event and reviewed weekly.

For sellers on our US marketplace in the 90 days after launch, I'd watch two things the team can move: how often sellers keep the AI text as-is, and time to publish a listing. Separately, for the business: conversion rate on AI-written listings and generation cost per description. Each publish event records whether the text was edited, and a weekly job reports the share.
North Star: weekly sellers who publish an AI description. We'd also look at revenue and engagement, and track everything in a dashboard.
I'd measure success by seller happiness and revenue growth across the company.
Looking at sellers on our marketplace over the first month, I'd track descriptions published without edits, listings per seller, and revenue.
Secondary: share of descriptions kept without edits. Business: cost per description. We'd log a 'description kept' event when a seller publishes without changing the text.

I wouldn't assume the new model is worse. I'd rerun our fixed set of test prompts on the old and new model and compare. I'd also check whether the switch shipped with prompt or IDE plugin changes, which would be an application-layer cause. I'd look at task completion and re-query rate, and check time-to-first-token and cost per query, since a bigger model is often slower.

Confirm first: run the same 300 benchmark tasks on the old and new model. Separate the model from what we built around it, like the system prompt or how we send code context. Check hallucinated APIs per suggestion and how often devs ask again. And latency: if the new model takes 3 seconds longer to start answering, people stop waiting.
The new model must be worse, so I'd ask engineering to switch back and keep an eye on satisfaction scores.
Usage drops happen. I'd send users a survey and add more features to win them back.
I'd compare the old and new model on the same test prompts to confirm. Then I'd watch task completion rate and how often developers re-ask.
